newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer, Waigel panic Germans on euro - Schmidt.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer, Waigel panic Germans on euro - Schmidt.

text.p: Former German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt on Wednesday accused Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer and finance minister Theo Waigel of unnerving already-panicky Germans over the single European currency.
"Their continual talk of 'stability' is leading to the impression that the euro cannot in fact bring this about," Schmidt said in an interview with the Rheinischer Merkur newspaper.
He added: "The finance minister and the Bundesbank president have seriously deepened people's scepticism (about currency union) without -- as I in all good faith hope -- meaning to."

Germany, led by Waigel, was the main sponsor of the "stability pact" agreed by finance ministers in Dublin last December, an accord intended to ensure a stable euro by punishing countries which overstep agreed economic convergence criteria after the planned EMU start in January 1999.

Schmidt pointed to recent controversies in Germany over everything from tax reform to plans for the new high-speed Transrapid train as showing that Germans were at the moment particularly susceptible to being panicked in this way.
"The Germans at the moment are against everything that is new. They are the European champions of fear," he said.

Schmidt has been particularly vociferous in recent months in his criticism of central bank chief Tietmeyer, whom he has accused of having a hidden agenda of actually wanting to stall European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

A Bundesbank spokesman said it had no immediate reaction to the interview. Tietmeyer himself was in Bonn to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the birth of the legendary German economist Ludwig Erhard, creator of the deutschemark.
Ordinary Germans meanwhile appear to be becoming increasingly worried about giving up their currency.

A poll published by the "Stern" magazine in December showed that 61 percent of Germans were now "fearful" of the euro, with only 16 percent "hopeful". Previous polls had indicated a slightly lower level of concern about the currency switch.

Schmidt, Germany's Social Democratic Chancellor from 1974 to 1982, further attacked the present Chancellor Helmut Kohl for not being able to grasp the mechanics governing monetary union sufficiently to influence the debate in Germany.
"He has got the right instincts, but he cannot convincingly express himself in this field because he understands too little about it," Schmidt said.
